blocks.text: Maturity is the ability to respond to the environment in an appropriate manner, usually with a learnt response - the production of expected, age-appropriate behaviour and actions in a given situation.
Psychosocial maturity is a key factor in the development of a sense of autonomy and includes processes involving cognitive, emotional, social and moral development.

Development is influenced by both nature (genetic disposition) and nurture (environmental influences); the proportional contribution of each to the psychosocial development of personality, intelligence and sexuality is fiercely debated.
Studies estimate a heritability of 40-==50%== for human **intelligence quotient**, but several observations warrant consideration.

blocks.title: Observations qualifying the heritability of intelligence quotient
rows: Heritability is around ==30%== in children and increases to ==80%== among adults - either genetic determinants of intelligence are age-specific, or non-genetic maturational factors are much more influential at younger ages.

Scarr et al. observed greater genetic effects on intelligence in middle-class white groups than in lower-class African American groups, suggesting non-genetic influences operate among lower socioeconomic groups. Irving Gottesman (proponent of the endophenotype concept) stated that genes are weaker than poverty.

Intelligence is made of several sub-constructs, so no single gene or genetic complex is likely to account for the variation; the genetic factors operating could also vary at different stages of development.

Genetic influence is inferred from closer biological relatives (e.g. identical twins) being more similar than less closely related pairs, but there is greater similarity between family members than predicted by biological relationship, indicating an effect of shared environment (Deary et al., 2010).

bullets.text: Maturity = ability to respond to the environment appropriately for age, usually with a learnt response.
Psychosocial maturity underpins autonomy and spans cognitive, emotional, social and moral development.
Nature (genes) and nurture (environment) both shape development; their proportional contribution is hotly debated.
Intelligence quotient heritability is estimated at 40-50%, but about 30% in children rising to 80% in adults.
Scarr: genetic effects on intelligence quotient greater in middle-class white than lower-class African American groups; Gottesman: genes are weaker than poverty.
Greater similarity within families than predicted by biological relationship points to a shared-environment effect (Deary 2010).

sections.title: 2. Stage theories, maturational tasks and the main developmental theories

blocks.text: Stage theories consider development as a process occurring over a 12- to 15-year period in chunks of time called stages. Within each stage a specific set of functioning and behaviour can be observed, and certain maturational tasks (motor, cognitive, perceptual) are achieved, heralding transition to the next stage.

Piaget's theory is a prototype stage theory focused on epistemology (the study of the development of knowledge or intelligence). According to Piaget, development (1) occurs in hierarchical stages, (2) each stage is qualitatively different (not just quantitatively), and (3) the stages consist of invariant functions and all children undergo these sequentially.
Other stage theorists include Gesell, Freud and Erikson.

blocks.title: Outline of developmental theories
rows: Temperaments are inherent biologically based traits varying from difficult to easy (or inhibited to uninhibited). Temperament elicits environmental response that perpetuates a pattern of behaviour.
Development occurs in stages, with transition occurring as a result of interaction of the child with its environment (child as a scientist).
Innate tendency to seek relationships influences patterns of behaviour in later life.
Observational learning in childhood influences later behaviour.
Stage-specific behaviours are driven by inner conflicts and resulting anxiety signals; successful resolution of conflicts aids progressive maturation.
Stages are characterized by conflicts, but successful resolution is not mandatory for further development.

Development is not entirely private; the child acts as an apprentice in social surroundings rather than a scientist. Parents and teachers provide scaffolding; the zone of proximal development refers to functions not yet fully achieved but in the 'pipeline', whose development is aided by scaffolding.
Maturation of the nervous system is the principal driver of the various aspects of human behaviour.

By 18 months: walks alone, up to 40 words, holophrases, rapprochement; 2 years: runs, tower of 6 cubes, parallel play.
Copying: cross at 3-4 years, triangle at 5, diamond at 6; 4 years skips, 5 years hops.

Clock reading: age 4-5 beginning to read the hour, 5-6 hour or half hour, 6-7 quarter hour (mock explanation).

blocks.text: Freud's model notes the gradual, sequential emergence of genital sexuality from infantile sexuality; the stages reflect both biological and psychological maturation.

blocks.caption: Table image: Freud's psychosexual stages and characteristics - Oral (0 to 1 1/2 years), Anal (1 1/2 to 3 years), Phallic/Oedipal (3 to 5 yrs), Latency (5 to puberty approx. 11 yrs), Genital (puberty onwards).

blocks.title: Freud's psychosexual stages
rows: Drive discharge is via sucking; oral erotogenic zone. Oral erotism (sucking, licking) in early stages; oral sadism (biting, chewing) in later stages. The ego develops at this stage.

Anal erotogenic zone; drive discharge via sphincter behaviour. Anal erotism = sexual pleasure in anal functioning; anal sadism = aggressive wishes linked to fecal expulsion. Anal fixation is characterized by **obsessive-compulsive disorder**-like pattern, with ambivalence and sadomasochistic tendencies.

Genitals become organs of interest; masturbation-like activity. Oedipus complex - wish for a libidinal relationship with the opposite-sex parent (Electra complex in girls) with a desire to exclude the rival parent; fear of retaliation = castration anxiety in boys, loss of mother's love in girls.
Socialization, interest in peers. Sexual energy sublimated towards school work, hobbies and friends.
Biological maturation occurs; genital sexuality is born.

blocks.mnemonic: OAPLG — Old Aunts Pour Lovely Gin

blocks.text: Electra complex in girls includes penis envy (a wish to have a penis, with blame of the mother for its absence); later this becomes a secret wish to displace mother as object of father's love and bear his baby.

At resolution of the Oedipus and Electra complexes, identification with the aggressor occurs (dad for a boy, mum for a girl) and the super-ego develops from introjection of parental values. Abraham divided the phallic phase into early partial genital (true phallic phase) and later mature genital phase.

A 4-year-old girl who now recognises she is a girl and wants more time with her father is in the **PHALLIC** phase (3-5 years) — the explanation ties it to penis envy, a wish to receive the penis and bear a child (the Electra complex), resolved by identification with the mother; genital, oral, anal and latency are the distractors.

Freud matching: establishment of trust = oral; strive for control = anal; castration anxiety and resolution of the oedipal complex = phallic; socialisation and interest in peers = latency; establishment of mature object relationships **AND** true self-identity = genital (one phase can be keyed to two descriptions).

Projection of good and bad impulses onto the mother followed by splitting is **NOT** a Freudian stage — it is Klein's paranoid-schizoid position.

Anal 1.5-3y: sphincter behaviour; anal fixation = obsessive-compulsive disorder-like pattern, ambivalence, sadomasochism.
Phallic 3-5y: Oedipus/Electra complex; castration anxiety (boys), loss of mother's love (girls).

blocks.text: A critical period is a time point when an individual is acutely sensitive to the effects of external influences, both positive and negative; it is related to the notion of gradually decreasing plasticity across the life span, though this is challenged by observations that, e.g., attachment can be formed even at later ages.

Early life is the period of most rapid brain development and so a sensitive phase for positive and adverse influences. Severe neglect (e.g. institutional care) produces adverse consequences if it occurs in early rather than later childhood; the effects of toxins (e.g. lead and alcohol) are far more dramatic when exposure occurs in utero or early life. Adolescence is also a critical period; major life transitions influencing development occur during adolescence.

Stress vulnerability model (Zubin & Spring, 1977): mental illness, schizophrenia especially, results from two hits - the first is vulnerability/predisposition (biologically or psychosocially determined), the second is the stress factor acting as trigger or precipitant (biological, psychological or social). Low-vulnerability individuals need a high degree of stress to develop illness; highly vulnerable individuals may respond to hairline triggers.

Caspi et al. (2003), gene-environment interaction: individuals with one or two copies of the short allele of the **serotonin transporter** promoter polymorphism showed more depressive symptoms, diagnosable depression and suicidality in relation to stressful life events than individuals homozygous for the long allele.

blocks.caption: Shaded box: STRESS VULNERABILITY MODEL (Zubin & Spring, 1977; two hits - vulnerability and stress factor) and the Caspi et al (2003) serotonin transporter promoter polymorphism study, as printed.

blocks.title: Three types of stress response in young children
rows: Brief, mild response moderated by the availability of a caring and responsive adult (e.g. an immunization, first day at nursery). When buffered adequately these are growth-promoting opportunities.

Exposure to non-normative experiences of greater magnitude of adversity (e.g. death of a family member, serious illness or injury). When buffered well, the risk of physiologic harm and long-term consequences is greatly reduced.

Strong, frequent or prolonged activation of the body's stress response in the absence of buffering protection from supportive adults (e.g. child abuse or neglect, parental substance abuse, maternal depression). Disrupts developing brain circuitry during sensitive periods, forming precursors of later physical and mental illness.

blocks.title: Methodology for studying development
rows: Children of different ages are compared on a behaviour to find age-specific features; inter-individual variations can distort the true picture.
The same children are studied twice or more over a prolonged period; gives more reliable estimates of development but is time-consuming.

A risk factor does not necessarily imply causation (could be a third variable, reverse causality or multivariate relationships); multivariate factors that partially account for the relationship between a risk factor and a disorder are mediators, which could be a protective factor or buffer.

bullets.text: Critical period = time of acute sensitivity to external influences; early life and adolescence are sensitive phases.
Severe neglect and toxins (lead, alcohol) are far more damaging in early life / in utero.
Zubin & Spring (1977) stress-vulnerability: first hit = vulnerability, second hit = stress trigger.
Caspi 2003: short allele of serotonin transporter promoter + stressful life events = more depression and suicidality.
Stress responses: positive (brief, buffered, growth-promoting) and tolerable (greater adversity; harm reduced if buffered well).
Toxic stress: strong, frequent or prolonged, no adult buffering; disrupts developing brain circuitry.
Cross-sectional = different ages compared; longitudinal = same children followed (more reliable, slower).

blocks.text: Bowlby: attachment begins in infancy and lasts a lifetime; the primary caregiver (usually, but not always, the mother) most shapes the child's personality and character. Strong bonds are formed within minutes of giving birth; too many individuals in the room right after birth can disrupt attachment, with long-term effects on the parent-child relationship (Klaus, Kennell & Klaus, 1995).

Attachment formation needs the caregiver's presence in early stages; no difference is made if motherly care is provided late (especially after 30 months) and not in the early stages. Attachment behaviour is more evident when distress is present.

Monotropy: Bowlby's strong innate tendency to attach to one adult female, qualitatively different from later attachments. But multiple attachments are the rule: around 18 months ==87%== of infants have multiple attachments (==50%== primarily attached to the mother, ==18%== to the father, the rest equally to both). The attachment process matters more than who the attachment figure is.

blocks.subtopic: Polytropy (more than one attachment figure)
blocks.note: Not covered in the Human Development notes — tested via an **extended matching item**: a child who has more than one attachment figure is described as showing polytropy, e.g. a 20-month-old who cries whenever mother, father or childminder says goodbye. (The notes give monotropy and state that multiple attachments are the rule, but do not name polytropy.)

blocks.text: Bowlby: attachment is innate and adaptive (an inherited need that helps survival; the helpless newborn relies on the caregiver for food and warmth). Attachment behaviour peaks between 12-18 months.

blocks.title: Phases of attachment
rows: Allows strangers to handle; infants become attached to one or more persons in the environment.
Preferential attachment, separation anxiety, object permanence, stranger anxiety; later, weakened stranger anxiety and other attachment figures may be present.
The mother figure is seen as independent.

blocks.text: Phases of attachment by vignette: a 10-week-old who orients to her mother = pre-attachment; a 5-month-old who allows strangers to handle her and is attached to mother, sister and grandmother = indiscriminate attachment; a 2-year-old with preferential attachment to mother who also attaches to father = clear-cut attachment (a 4th phase from 25 months sees the mother as independent).

blocks.text: Harlow's experiments established contact comfort as basic as the need for food in mother-infant bonding. Rhesus monkeys separated from their mothers preferred a cloth-covered surrogate (contact comfort) to a wire surrogate, irrespective of feeding - even if the cloth surrogate had no feeding nipple.

blocks.subtopic: Age at which the Strange Situation is used
blocks.note: Not covered in the Human Development notes — tested via the mock exams: the Strange Situation study of attachment was carried out on children aged 12-24 months; the infant's reactions are noted in three phases: reaction to a stranger with the mother present, reaction when left alone with a stranger, and reaction on re-union with the mother. The notes give the seven situations but no age.

blocks.text: The Strange Situation contains 2 separation and 2 re-union episodes within seven combinations of mother/stranger presence, and the infant is classified A anxious avoidant, B secure or C anxious resistant; the distractors vary the counts (1 and 3, 2 and 3, 3 and 1, 1 and 2).

The classification correlates highly with (1) responsiveness and sensitivity of the mothers to their children's needs and (2) total amount and quality of stimulation (holding) provided by the mothers.

blocks.title: Ainsworth attachment types
rows: Indifferent to mother leaving or entering; keeps playing. Distress when alone, not when mother leaves. Stranger can comfort easily. Highly environment directed, low attachment behaviour. Greater in the West. Perpetrators of bullying mostly have this pattern.
Plays independently when mother is near (secure base effect). Distress when mother leaves; seeks contact on her return and is quickly comforted by the mother, not a stranger.

Fussy, cries a lot, cannot use mother as secure base. Very high distress at mother leaving, not comforted easily on return; ambivalent; actively resists stranger's efforts. Highly caregiver directed, low play behaviour. Greater in Japanese and Israeli families. Common among victims of bullying.

blocks.text: A 2-year-old who keeps playing when her mother leaves and shows no response when she returns = **ANXIOUS** **AVOIDANT** attachment (explanation: indifferent to mother leaving or entering; distress when left alone is comforted by a stranger rather easily) — not secure, resistant, disorganised or absent attachment.

Showing no distress at the mother's leaving and ignoring her on return is keyed to insecurely attached **ANXIOUS** **AVOIDANT** behaviour; this explanation quotes about ==20%== for avoidant children whereas the types table gives ==15%==, and the 'anxious ambivalent' and 'anxious resistant' distractors both describe the type C pattern (distress, resisting comfort) rather than indifference.

Strange Situation vignettes: strong initial proximity seeking followed by high avoidance, with the child frightened, distressed and frozen on the mother's return = **DISORGANISED**; busy exploring, minimal distress at separation and ignoring the caregiver on reunion = **AVOIDANT**; high distress on separation, angry approach, resisting comfort and slow to settle = **RESISTANT**/**AMBIVALENT**. The explanation states the procedure was devised with 12- to 18-month infants.

blocks.text: **DISORGANISED** attachment is the pattern commonly reported in abused children — Main and Solomon (1990) added it as a fourth category for children who did not fit Ainsworth's three; about ==15%== of children in middle-class non-clinical groups show it, it is more frequent in maltreated or maternally deprived children, and the mother may herself have been abused. Avoidant, secure, multiple and ambivalent are the distractors.

Type D - disorganised: seen in maltreated or maternally deprived children. The child has an insecure, dazed look and acts as if frightened of the mother; may be a precursor to later personality difficulties or dissociative experiences. The mother may have been abused as a child.
Attachment style may differ with different caregivers; it is a function of the quality of caregiving and **NOT** the temperament of the child.

Main devised a semi-structured Adult Attachment Interview with 15 items, based on the fact that the infantile attachment pattern can be predicted reasonably accurately using discourse analysis of adults when recollecting their childhood. Four patterns are noted.

blocks.title: Main's Adult Attachment Interview: four patterns
rows: Spontaneous, coherent answers; can talk freely about negative experiences in childhood
Minimise experiences, do not elaborate, no colourful metaphors
Multiple emotionally laden responses; ramble excessively (insecure ambivalent/enmeshed)
Broken continuity; interrupted logical flow of thoughts

blocks.text: Adult Attachment Interview vignettes: spontaneous, coherent, non-defensive answers able to discuss negative experiences = **AUTONOMOUS** (secure); minimising, brief answers, 'I don't remember', no colourful metaphors = **DISMISSING** (explanation adds idealising caregivers); outpouring of emotion, lengthy childhood memories, angry/tearful or overwhelmed = **ENTANGLED** (the explanation also calls it preoccupied).

blocks.text: Secure attachment appears protective for childhood disorders; insecure attachment is a risk factor. Insecure attachment in early childhood is associated with behavioural problems, especially oppositional defiant disorder at school age, and in combination with family dysfunction, difficult temperament and poor parental management can give rise to later childhood disorders.

Spitz - anaclitic depression (hospitalism): when children are hospitalised for physical problems, the short separation from the primary caregiver (object loss) is counterproductive to development. Recovery is good if maternal deprivation is kept to under 3 months; rare if prolonged. Surrogate mothering helps to some extent.

Short separation from the primary caregiver when hospitalised for a physical problem = **ANACLITIC** depression (Spitz, hospitalism; object loss) — **NOT** privation (non-formation of attachment), deprivation (Rutter), pathological separation anxiety or a childhood grief reaction; recovery is good if maternal deprivation is kept to less than three months.

sections.title: 6. Mahler's separation-individuation, deprivation vs privation, and ethology

blocks.text: Mahler described the development of a sense of identity in young children, independent of their mothers (separation-individuation theory); the proposed stages are supposed to be universal in all children.

blocks.caption: Boxed list: MAHLER'S STAGES - 1. Normal autism (0 to 2 m); 2. Symbiosis (2 to 5m); 3. Separation-individuation phase (DPRO) with sub-phases a) Differentiation (5 to 10m), b) Practicing (10 to 18m), c) Rapprochement (18 to 24m), d) Object constancy (2 to 5yrs).

blocks.title: Mahler's stages
rows: Child spends most time in sleep, as if the intrauterine aloofness continues.
Inner and outer world studied via the senses; perceives mother and self as one unit.
Slowly appreciates the difference between mother and self.
Gradual increase in interest in the environment; practices exploration.
Alternating drives to be autonomous and dependent; can explore alone but requires comfort and reassurance on return.
Understands the mother will not be lost if temporarily away; able to function independently.

blocks.text: The newborn phase in Mahler's theory is **NORMAL** **AUTISM** (0-2 months: mostly sleep, as if intrauterine aloofness continues) — not symbiosis (2-5 months), rapprochement, object constancy or the umbrella separation-individuation phase.

Mahler vignettes: a 1-month-old sleeping most of the time = normal autism; an 18-month-old with alternating drives to be autonomous and dependent who explores alone but needs comfort on the mother's return = rapprochement sub-phase; a 3-year-old who understands the mother will not be lost if temporarily away and so functions independently = object constancy sub-phase.

blocks.subtopic: Mahler later discarded the term "normal autistic phase"
blocks.note: Not covered in the Human Development notes — tested via the mock exams: the first few weeks of infancy are termed the 'normal autistic phase' (Mahler later discarded this designation): the newborn is blissfully unaware of anything but its own needs and the mother needs to be available to meet them.

blocks.title: Rutter: deprivation vs privation
rows: Attachment is formed but lost temporarily. Short separation: protest - despair - detachment phases (similar to grief); more common at 8 months to 3 years; boys show more features than girls; more noticeable if aggressive caregiving (e.g. physical abuse) preceded separation. Prolonged deprivation: separation anxiety, clinginess, psychosomatic complaints, vacillation and aggression.

Non-formation of attachment; very rare. Can lead to 'affectionless psychopathy' and developmental retardation: attention seeking, lack of guilt, antisocial behaviour, indiscriminate attachment. Reversible only to some extent.

blocks.text: Ethology is the systematic biological study of animal behaviour (Greek ethos - custom or habit), a term coined by Heinroth.

Imprinting is a special primitive form of learning in which, during an early critical or sensitive phase, a young animal is highly sensitive to a certain stimulus that provokes a specific behaviour pattern. Lorenz described it in goslings (following the first moving object); when Lorenz presented himself as the moving object, the goslings followed him and refused to follow mother goose. Imprinting is particularly resistant to change.

**Innate releasing mechanism**: sensory mechanism selectively responsive to a specific external stimulus and responsible for triggering the stereotyped motor response. **Fixed action pattern**: an inherent, species-specific, stereotyped pattern of behaviour initiated by specific stimuli (e.g. following behaviour in goslings).

items.text: Mahler is the theorist associated with the autistic phase (normal autism) and with separation-individuation (distractors: conventional morality, anal phase, operational stage, individuality vs inferiority).
The theory of identity development in children independent of their mothers = Margaret Mahler (distractors Freud, Rutter, Spitz, Winnicott).
'Inner and outer world studied via the senses but mother and self perceived as one unit' = **SYMBIOSIS** (2-5 months), not normal autism (0-2 months, mostly sleeping).
A 28-month-old who can stay alone for long but runs to hug her mother on return from work is keyed to **RAPPROCHEMENT** (anxious about loss of the caregiver's love despite new skills).

items.text: Infants who do not interact with the mother when she is present and are not upset when left with the stranger are **ANXIOUS**/**AVOIDANT** (not resistant or disorganised; 'all of the above' is a distractor).
A securely attached child shows discomfort when the mother leaves but **NOT** for being alone (the reverse pattern, upset when alone but not at her absence, is avoidant).
The most common attachment type in the Western world is **SECURE** (most children are securely attached), even though the types table notes avoidant is greater in the West than elsewhere.

bullets.text: Mahler: normal autism 0-2m, symbiosis 2-5m, then separation-individuation (differentiation 5-10m, practicing 10-18m, rapprochement 18-24m, object constancy 2-5y).
Rapprochement = alternating drives to be autonomous and dependent; object constancy = mother understood as not lost when away.
Rutter deprivation: attachment formed then lost; protest-despair-detachment; commoner at 8m-3y.
Rutter privation: attachment never formed; affectionless psychopathy; only partly reversible.
Imprinting (Lorenz, goslings): early critical-phase learning, particularly resistant to change.
Innate releasing mechanism triggers a stereotyped motor response; fixed action pattern is a species-specific stereotyped behaviour pattern.
Mahler's 0-2 month 'normal autistic phase': newborn aware only of its own needs; she later discarded the label.

blocks.text: Object relations theory: the ego exists only in relation to other objects, which may be external or internal; 'object' refers to both living persons and non-living concepts. Melanie Klein was a major proponent; others include Fairbairn, Kernberg, Guntrip, Winnicott and Balint.

blocks.title: Kleinian theory
rows: Play interpretation was the major technique employed.
Maintained that oedipal development occurred earlier than Freud envisaged.
An infant possessed instinctual knowledge of the body.
Not age specific, but the paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions are said to occur between 0-3 months (very early).

blocks.caption: Flowchart: 'A flowchart describing Kleinian theory of infant's ('object-') relationship with the mother' - four boxes joined by downward arrows: fear of annihilation and projection of destructive impulse; projection and splitting (paranoid-schizoid position); realisation of the unified object, weaning and guilt (depressive position); reparation phase (manic defense in absence of reparation).

blocks.title: Klein's flowchart of the infant's relationship with the mother
rows: Present soon after birth; intolerable, so the child projects this destructive impulse onto external objects.
Projection of bad and good impulses, then splitting of the external world into good and bad (cannot unify them); bad objects include nongratifying bad breasts (parts); leads to persecutory anxiety.

Child realizes good and bad emanate from one unified object (whole); weaning occurs and is perceived as a loss; guilt for destructive impulses against the mother; fear of loss of the love of the object.

Creativity emanates as an attempt to repair the damage done by the destructive impulse; continues lifelong. Without reparation a maladaptive manic defense can emerge: denial of reality (refusal to take guilt), omnipotence and grandiosity.

blocks.title: Winnicott's concepts
rows: Psychological development occurs in a zone between reality and fantasy; play is an important aspect of development.

Soft toy, towel or similar object helping transition from ideal objects of fantasy to real objects; buffers against loss, is invested with the primary object's qualities (e.g. mother's contact) but remains under the child's control.
A mother need not be perfect but good enough to provide a growth-sustaining environment (holding).
Parental control and impositions can lead to a false self, different from the real self (theory of multiple self-organizations).

bullets.text: Object relations: ego exists only in relation to internal/external objects; Klein, Fairbairn, Kernberg, Guntrip, Winnicott, Balint.
Klein: play interpretation; earlier oedipal development than Freud; weaning symbolically equals castration.
Kleinian defences SIPDOG: splitting, introjection, projective identification, denial, omnipotence, grandiosity.
Paranoid-schizoid position: splitting good/bad, persecutory anxiety; depressive position: whole object, weaning loss, guilt, fear of loss of love.
Reparation = creativity repairing damage; absent reparation gives manic defense (denial, omnipotence, grandiosity).
Winnicott: transitional object, good enough mother (holding), false self from parental control.

blocks.text: Parenting style is a psychological construct of standard strategies parents use in child rearing, including the demands of children and responses of parents. Quality of care is more important than quantity of time spent; parenting practices are specific behaviours.

blocks.caption: 2x2 table: Responsive/Unresponsive against Demanding/Undemanding - Authoritative/Propagative, Indulgent (Permissive), Authoritarian/Totalitarian, Neglectful.

blocks.title: Parenting styles (Maccoby and Martin; Baumrind described 3 response patterns)

blocks.caption: Table image: Control, Nurturance, Maturity demands and Communication for Authoritative, Authoritarian, Permissive and Neglecting parenting.

blocks.title: Features of parenting styles
rows: High degree of nurturance and leniency
Age-appropriate demands placed on growing child
High degree of demands placed on growing child
No demands placed on growing child

blocks.text: Authoritative parenting: parents are demanding but responsive; fits propagative parenting and concerted cultivation. Indulgent parenting (low demand, high response): parents try to be friends with the child; as adults, those with indulgent parents pay less attention to avoiding behaviours which cause aggression in others. Authoritarian parenting is restrictive and punishment-heavy, rules followed without explanation. Neglectful parents are detached and dismissive, not involved in the child's life, and also dismiss the child's emotions and opinions.

Parents who set **NO** limits, with poor impulse control and aggression when boundaries are violated = **PERMISSIVE**. The explanation contrasts authoritarian (strict rules; low self-esteem, social withdrawal), neglectful (poor self-esteem, impaired self-control, increased aggression) and authoritative (firm rules with shared decision-making; self-reliance, positive self-esteem); 'good enough parent' is a distractor.

blocks.title: Birth order
rows: More parental time; higher **intelligence quotient**; more achievement driven; more authoritarian, conservative and conformist.
Receive the least attention at home; strong peer relationships.
Receive most attention, get 'spoiled'; independent and rebellious.

blocks.text: Family structure: children with single parents or in large families have more behavioural issues; single-sex couples and extended family involvement in upbringing do not cause the same issues. Family dysfunction causes discord and rejection of children via disengagement and/or overprotection and over-involvement (enmeshment).

Family instability: **HYPERACTIVE** children are more affected than easy-going ones is the correct statement; the explanation also says boys are affected more than girls and younger children more than older children (so 'boys less affected' and 'younger less affected' are wrong), cognitive achievement is affected, and the most common psychopathology is behavioural difficulty — not psychosis.

Cambridge Study of Delinquent Development (Farrington et al.): the most important childhood predictors (age 8-10) of delinquency were antisocial child behaviour, impulsivity, low intelligence, low attainment, family criminality, poverty and poor parent-child rearing behaviour.

Parental loss: most children adapt well to parental divorce if financial support, reasonable contact with the non-custodial parent and successful remarriage of the single parent occur. If not: poor academic achievement, low self-esteem, 2-3 times more antisocial behaviour and higher rates of later-life depression.

blocks.title: Effects of parental divorce
rows: Short-term behavioural difficulties; even infants may show changes in eating, sleeping and bowel patterns, with fearful or anxious responses.
Often assume responsibility for the parental separation.
Feel hurt, become angry and critical of parents; spend most time away from home.
Recovery usually takes 3 to 5 years; one third of all children have lasting psychological effects.
Boys are more affected than girls; among boys, physical aggression is a common sign of distress.

Recent divorce/separation predicts suicide in children; ==25%== of step families dissolve in 2 years whereas ==75%== are harmonious; **attention deficit hyperactivity disorder**, antisocial **personality disorder** and conduct problems are more common in homes without a father.

blocks.text: 'Increased motivation for academic performance' is the **NOT**-an-effect of parental separation — the explanation says academic and social aptitude suffers; guilt/accepting responsibility, suicidal ideas, physical aggression and changes in bowel habits are the options treated as effects (infants may change eating, sleeping and bowel patterns).

Children of divorced parents divorce twice as often as children of undivorced parents; academic and social aptitude suffers; asthma, injuries, headaches and speech defects are more common. Divorce has more impact than death of a parent on the child's psychological make-up, and parental death has somewhat lesser impact than parental conflict and separation. Suicide rates for children of divorce are very high; ==25%== have adjustment problems as teenagers.

Bereavement increases temper tantrums, depressive reaction (sadness, irritability) and sleep disturbance; divorce can cause all of these, but protective factors include positive temperament, relationship with siblings and joint access.
Day care: care for more than 4 months at less than 1 year of age for more than 20 hours a week can increase insecure attachment; otherwise day care does not affect development adversely.

Day care is detrimental only in a specific dose: at least 20 hours per week for 4 months or more before the first birthday increases insecure attachment (Belsky and Rovine, 1988) — the distractors (day care reduces attachment behaviour, induces neurotic clinging, affects cognitive development, increases maternal bonding) are the distractors.

Adoption: the earlier the age of adoption the better the outcome; children adopted before age 4 or 5 generally do well. When a child is adopted during early childhood, the chances of forming new attachments are better; early adoption is therefore recommended as a matter of social policy. Late adoption after age 8 does not necessarily lead to adjustment problems, but such children are more vulnerable to behavioural problems at home and school (Tizard and Hodges 1978). Adopted children usually become aware of their status between 2 and 4 years; parental disclosure reduces later psychological trauma.

Institutional care (Tizard and Hodges): children in institutions from infancy, looked after by a number of frequently changing carers, and adopted at age 4 had formed reasonably good attachments to adoptive parents by age 8; at age 16 they showed the ex-institutional syndrome - related better to adults than to peers, less likely to have a special friend, less selective in choosing friends, and turned to peers less often for emotional support.
Intrafamilial abuse: sexual abuse by a parent can result in anxiety-related symptoms, sexualized behaviour, borderline personality disorder, substance misuse, dissociation and depression.

blocks.subtopic: Protective factors against child abuse
blocks.note: Not covered in the Human Development notes — tested via the mock exams: emotionally satisfying relationships with a network of relatives or friends protect against child abuse; parents who were abused as children are less likely to abuse their own children if they have resolved internal conflicts and pain about their history and have an intact, stable, supportive, non-abusive relationship with their partner. Parental personality disorder, history of maltreatment, high parental expectations and young parental age were the distractors.

blocks.subtopic: Single-parent households and child abuse
blocks.note: Not covered in the Human Development notes — tested via the mock exams: the rate of child abuse in single-parent households is 27.3 per 1,000 children, nearly twice that in two-parent households (15.5 per 1,000) (Goldman et al., 2003). The notes link single parenthood to behavioural issues but give no abuse rates.

bullets.text: Four styles: authoritative (demanding, responsive), authoritarian (demanding, unresponsive), indulgent (undemanding, responsive), neglectful (undemanding, unresponsive).
Quality of care matters more than quantity of time.
Birth order: first-borns higher intelligence quotient, achievement driven; middle-borns least attention, strong peer ties; last-borns spoiled, independent, rebellious.
Cambridge study: predictors of delinquency at 8-10 include antisocial behaviour, impulsivity, low intelligence quotient, family criminality, poverty, poor child rearing.
Divorce: recovery usually 3-5 years; one third have lasting effects; boys more affected.
Day care over 4 months, under 1 year, over 20 h/week can increase insecure attachment.
Earlier adoption = better outcome; adoption before 4-5 years generally does well; late adoption after 8 carries more risk.
Ex-institutional syndrome (Tizard and Hodges): better with adults than peers, no special friend, non-selective friendships.
Child-abuse protective factors: network of relatives/friends; resolved parental history with stable supportive partner (mock).

facts.label: Children with lasting effects after divorce
Step families that dissolve within 2 years

blocks.text: Temperament is an aspect of personality studied in infants, describing individual differences in behavioural style. Infant negative emotionality (e.g. fear) and reactions to new situations (inhibition or neophobia) are the two most stable temperaments.
New York Longitudinal Study (Thomas & Chess): a thirty-year (initially 6-year) longitudinal study of 138 children using parental interviews to ascertain temperamental dimensions.

blocks.forTopic: Thomas and Chess's nine temperamental dimensions
blocks.mnemonic: ARAAITMDA — Active Rabbits Approach Armadillos Inquisitively, Treading Mostly Dainty Aisles

blocks.title: Three behavioural styles identified
rows: Rhythmic pattern of needs, adapts well, active
Less predictable, uncomfortable with new experiences, negative mood, reacts intensely to stimuli, difficult to comfort
Adapts poorly to change, but less active and responds at low intensity

blocks.text: Difficult temperament may offer some survival benefits, as the mother pays more attention - especially in tribal populations. Inhibition (approach/withdrawal dimension) is, according to Kagan, a strongly inborn trait; behavioural inhibition may be a precursor for later neurotic disorders including anxiety and depression. In extreme inhibition (neophobia) a child appears frozen and withdrawn in novel situations.

Goodness of fit (Thomas & Chess): the reciprocal relationship between a baby's temperament and its social environment; a good match results in positive development later (used especially for the harmonious mother-child interaction).
Note: do not confuse with good-enough mothering (Winnicott) - mothers provide a holding environment; a mother does not need to be perfect but must provide good-enough mothering (see section 7).

**Emotionality-Activity-Sociability** model (Buss & Plomin 1984): three major dimensions - Emotionality, Activity, Sociability; a strongly biological model viewing temperament as inherited personality traits exhibited in early life.

Resilience is the ability of children to function well in the face of adversity: either (1) a positive psychological outcome in the face of adversity, or (2) a dynamic process of psychological functioning that increases positive and reduces adverse outcomes (Cummings, Davies & Campbell, 2000).

blocks.title: Factors conveying resilience (Masten and Coatsworth, 1998, and notes)
rows: Good intellectual functioning; appealing, sociable, easygoing disposition; self-efficacy, self-confidence, high self-esteem; talents; faith. Masten and Coatsworth (1998) described these factors in children faced with highly adverse situations (e.g. parental mental illness, family violence, poverty, natural disasters).
Close relationship with a caring parent figure; authoritative parenting (warmth, structure, high expectations); higher socioeconomic status; extended family networks.
Bonds to supportive adults outside the family; attachment to prosocial organizations; attending efficient schools/institutions.

bullets.text: Most stable temperaments: negative emotionality (fear) and inhibition/neophobia.
New York Longitudinal Study: 138 children, 30 years, 9 dimensions (activity ... attention span/persistence).
Styles: easy 40%, difficult 10%, slow to warm up 15%, ungrouped 35%.
Inhibition: strongly inborn (Kagan); precursor of anxiety and depression; neophobia = frozen and withdrawn in novelty.
Goodness of fit: good match of temperament and environment predicts positive development.
Emotionality-Activity-Sociability model (Buss & Plomin 1984): Emotionality, Activity, Sociability - inherited traits.
Resilience factors: personal (intelligence quotient, sociable, self-efficacy), family (caring parent, authoritative parenting, socioeconomic status), extrafamilial (supportive adults, schools).

Profiles (extended matching item): easy = regular rhythm, positive approach, rapid adaptation; slow to warm up = initial withdrawal, slow adaptation, mild intensity; difficult = negative withdrawal, intense negative mood, irregular.

blocks.text: Erikson's psychosocial stages coincide with Freud's psychosexual stages but extend well beyond adolescence. It is not necessary that each stage be resolved entirely before further progress; a mixture of positive and negative outcomes is noted for most people, but predominantly negative experiences accumulating at various stages may predispose to difficulties in life.

blocks.caption: Table: Erikson's Crisis and Approximate Age - 1. Basic trust vs. basic mistrust (birth to 12-18 months) through 8. Ego integrity vs. despair (late adulthood).

blocks.mnemonic: TAIIIIGI — Tiny Ants In Industrial Iron Imprisoned Giant Insects

blocks.subtopic: Erikson's virtue for each stage
blocks.note: Not covered in the Human Development notes — tested via an **extended matching item**: the virtues associated with the eight stages are hope, will, purpose, competence, fidelity, love, care and wisdom; the matching key pairs Trust vs mistrust = hope, Autonomy vs shame and doubt = will, Identity vs role confusion = fidelity, Intimacy vs isolation = love, Generativity vs stagnation = care, Integrity vs despair = wisdom.

blocks.mnemonic: HWPC-FLCW — Happy Wombats Plan Carefully; Foxes Love Caring Wisely

blocks.text: Autonomy refers to children gaining more control over activities and acquiring new skills; crucial for self-esteem, failing which a sense of shame is felt.

Industry (6 to 12 years): capable of learning, creating and accomplishing new skills and knowledge; a very social stage - unresolved feelings of inadequacy and inferiority among peers can cause serious problems with competence and self-esteem.

Identity vs. role confusion occurs in adolescence (approx. 12 to 18). Up to this stage development mostly depends on what is done to us; from teenage onwards it depends primarily on what we do. Teens develop a sense of self and personal identity and experiment with different social roles; the transition is associated with confusion and insecurity.

Young adulthood: the inherent strength is love and the major task is intimacy and formation of a future bond partner. Middle age: satisfaction through productivity in career and family/social network (generativity).
Older adult: reviews and cherishes life accomplishments and prepares for the end of life by pursuing lifelong interests (integrity).

Between ages 6 and 11 the Erikson crisis is **INDUSTRY** vs **INFERIORITY** (not autonomy vs shame, initiative vs guilt, trust vs mistrust or identity vs role confusion); this question quotes 6-11 and its explanation 6-12, whereas the stage table says 6 to 12.

blocks.subtopic: Intimacy vs isolation: age window and link to identity
blocks.note: Not covered in the Human Development notes — tested via the mock exams: the intimacy vs isolation conflict is placed at ages 20 to 40 (emphasised around age 30); at its start identity vs role confusion is coming to an end though it still lingers at the foundation of the stage (Erikson, 1950). The notes say only young adulthood.

blocks.text: A 22-year-old man = **INTIMACY** vs **ISOLATION** (young adulthood, 20-40 years; outcomes love and commitment vs superficial relationships) — not identity vs role confusion, the adolescent crisis that sits next to it as a distractor.

The **LAST** Erikson stage is **INTEGRITY** vs despair (old age); every wrong option also begins with 'I' (initiative vs guilt, identity vs identity confusion, industry vs inferiority, intimacy vs isolation), so read the whole label rather than the initial.

Erikson vignettes: a 3-year-old insisting on opening the door himself and crying when helped = **AUTONOMY** vs **SHAME** and doubt (18 months-3 years); a 50-year-old saving to help her children leave home = **GENERATIVITY** vs **STAGNATION** (about 40-60 years); a 72-year-old retired psychiatrist travelling, reading and doing limited private work = **INTEGRITY** vs **DESPAIR**.

bullets.text: Erikson's stages extend beyond adolescence; resolving each completely is not mandatory.
Trust vs mistrust (birth-12/18 mo); autonomy vs shame (18 mo-3 y); initiative vs guilt (3-6 y); industry vs inferiority (6-12 y).
Identity vs role confusion (adolescence, approx. 12-18); intimacy vs isolation (young adulthood); generativity vs stagnation (middle age); ego integrity vs despair (late adulthood).
Autonomy = control over activities; failure gives shame. Industry stage failure gives inferiority.
From adolescence onwards development depends primarily on what we do.
Erikson virtues: hope, will, purpose, competence, fidelity, love, care, wisdom (extended matching item).

blocks.text: A schema is the basic building block of intelligent behaviour, consisting of organized past experiences used to understand future experiences (physical schema such as bike riding; mental schemas such as addition).

Within each stage functioning is generally internally consistent and stable (equilibrium). Stage-to-stage transformation occurs through interaction with the environment when existing schemas cannot solve environmental realities.

Adaptation is fitting schemas to environmental information, by assimilation (new information incorporated into existing schemas without restructuring) or accommodation (schemas restructured to accommodate new information). Equilibration is achieved when all information fits the schemas; each time it occurs the child produces more effective schemata.

blocks.title: Piaget's stages
rows: Exercising reflexes (0-1 m); primary circular reactions (1-4 m) where reflexes extend to objects; secondary circular (4-10 m) where goal direction is seen; object permanence starts by 9 m; tertiary circular reactions (12-18 m) where novelty is sought; mental combinations occur; thoughts dominate actions.
Preconceptual stage 2 to 4 years; intuitive stage 4 to 7 years.
Ability to decentre, conserve, seriate; declining egocentrism; perspective taking starts to develop. Transitivity tasks (e.g. '4>2, 2>1, which is the greatest of all?') still difficult.

Manipulation of ideas and propositions (1st order operations); reasoning solely on verbal argument develops (2nd order operations). Hypothetico-deductive reasoning develops in a proportion of children after age 12.

blocks.text: Sensorimotor stage features - symbolic thought (language starts developing; thought starts to dominate actions); representational play (mimics one object with another, e.g. cup for a hat); deferred imitation (remembers an act and replays it later); recognition of self (primitive); object permanence.

Object permanence: understanding that an object that disappears from perception has not ceased to exist, so peek-a-boo is understood and enjoyed. Initially hidden objects are searched for where they were last seen (about 9 to 12 months), not where hidden; around 18 months invisible displacements are inferred and object permanence is complete.

Peek-a-boo is characteristic of the **SENSORIMOTOR** stage: object permanence arrives at about nine months, so the child understands an object that disappears has not ceased to exist (informal/formal operations, preoperational and concrete operations are the distractors).

blocks.title: Preoperational stage features
rows: Objects referred to by their function rather than appearance.
'Sky is blue because someone painted it'.
Cats have 4 legs, dogs have 4 legs, so cats and dogs are the same (Von Domarus law).
No functional propositions but verbs and nouns are used.
Causality inferred if two events occur with temporal association (lightning brings rain).
See moral development (spelt 'imminent' in some notes; correct term is immanent).
Lack of seriation, conservation and reversibility

Seriation = sorting/categorising by dimensional variations; centration = only a single dimension focused on at once (akin to syncretic thought). Conservation = a quantity (count, weight, volume) is unchanged if the same amount of material is transformed into a different shape. Compensation = magnification in one dimension and reduction in another nullify each other. Reversibility = mentally understanding that what is done can be undone without loss of material.
**NOT** selfishness - restricted ability to view the world from a single point of view; shown by the Mountains task (child cannot say what a person on the other side would see).
Signifiers (symbols and signs) represent something else, e.g. drawing a matchstick man; vital for developing play.
Links neighbouring objects and events on the basis of common instances (red square with red sphere with blue sphere with blue cube).

blocks.text: A 4-year-old who 'hides' an object on his head, assuming others cannot see it because he cannot, shows **EGOCENTRISM** (pre-operational, demonstrated with the mountains task) — not artificialism, propositional thought, precausal reasoning or circular reaction.

The mismatched pairing is 'Conservation tasks — sensorimotor stage': the explanation uses the mountain and conservation tasks to show the deficiencies of **PRE**-operational thinking; hiding objects = sensorimotor, classification by rules = concrete operational, pendulum = formal operational and mountain tasks = pre-operational are the correct pairs.

blocks.subtopic: Piaget's experiments by stage
blocks.note: Not covered in the Human Development notes — tested via an **extended matching item**: sensorimotor stage = peek-a-boo (object permanence); pre-operational stage = the three-mountains task (egocentrism: the child describes the doll's view as the same as their own) and conservation failures; concrete operational stage = classification of objects according to rules (serialising, ordering, grouping into classes); formal operational stage = the pendulum experiment (systematically examining length, weight, force and height of drop = hypothetico-deductive reasoning).

blocks.text: Concrete operational stage: conservation of liquid develops around 6 years, followed by length, count, weight and volume (around 11 to 12 years) in a vertical decalage fashion (one by one, not in parallel).

If the same question about quantity is asked before and after manipulating the material, the child answers differently the second time, interpreting the repeat as meaning the first answer was wrong; dropping the pre-transformation question, or using an external 'accident' (a naughty teddy disturbing a heap of coins), demonstrates conservation earlier than Piaget thought.

**Extended matching item** cross-theory matching by age: a 9-month-old = Trust vs mistrust + Sensorimotor + Oral; a 4-year-old = Pre-operational + Initiative vs guilt + Phallic; a 17-year-old = Deductive reasoning + Genital stage. The explanation gives sensorimotor 0-2 years, pre-operational 2-7, concrete operational 7-11, formal operational over 11, with hypothetico-deductive reasoning in a proportion after age 12.

blocks.subtopic: Theory of mind: age of onset
blocks.note: Not covered in the Human Development notes — tested via the mock exams: theory of mind develops at about age 4: children begin to understand that what people think, believe and desire affects how they behave, and 4-year-olds pass the false belief task because they understand that beliefs interpret the world rather than being direct copies. (The notes mention Theory of Mind only in the moral-development section, with no age.)

blocks.subtopic: Earliest retrievable memory and infantile amnesia
blocks.note: Not covered in the Human Development notes — tested via the mock exams: the average age of the earliest retrieved memory is 3.5 years; there is a total lack of memories for events in the first few years of life and amnesia for events in the first 2 to 5 years (infantile amnesia).

items.text: Piaget is the theorist of cognitive development (distractors Sullivan, Ainsworth, Munroe, Fromm); assimilation, accommodation, equilibration and schemas are his key concepts.
Object permanence develops in the **SENSORIMOTOR** stage (birth to 2): the baby differentiates self from objects and begins to act intentionally.
Deductive (hypothetico-deductive) reasoning = **FORMAL** operational stage, achieved in a proportion of children only after age 12 — the generic option 'operational stage' is a distractor.
A 4-year-old asking 'When do clouds sleep, papa?' shows **ANIMISM** (life and consciousness attributed to inanimate objects), not semiotic thinking, lack of conservation or egocentricity.

Recognising two balls as the same size despite a distance illusion = **CONCRETE** operational (conservation); this explanation says conservation of number, quantity and volume is achieved by 7-8 years, whereas the notes place liquid conservation at about 6 years.

**Extended matching item** theorist matching: Kohlberg = good boy-good girl and authority orientation; Freud = anal and genital stages; Erikson = autonomy-shame and integrity-despair; Mahler = symbiotic and autistic stages.

bullets.text: Schema = basic unit of intelligent behaviour; adaptation by assimilation (no restructuring) or accommodation (restructuring); equilibration.
Sensorimotor 0-2y; pre-operational 2-7y (preconceptual 2-4, intuitive 4-7); concrete operational 7-11y; formal operational over 11y.
Object permanence: hidden objects searched where last seen at 9-12 months; complete around 18 months.
Pre-operational: functional attribution, artificialism, animism, transductive reasoning, phenomenalistic causality, lack of conservation.
Egocentrism (Mountains task) is restricted single-viewpoint thinking, not selfishness.
Concrete operational: decentring, conservation, seriation; transitivity still hard.
Formal operational: ideas and propositions manipulated; hypothetico-deductive reasoning develops in a proportion of children after age 12.
Conservation of liquid about 6y, then length, count, weight, volume (11-12y) - vertical decalage; earlier if question design changed.
Piaget's experiments: peek-a-boo (sensorimotor), mountains (pre-operational), classification (concrete), pendulum (formal) (extended matching item).

bullets.text: Theory of mind develops at about 4 years (false belief task) (mock).
Earliest memory averages 3.5 years; infantile amnesia for the first 2-5 years (mock).

blocks.text: Basic speech sounds are phonemes (46 in English); most children can differentiate speech sounds before being able to produce them. The basic meaningful part of language is the morpheme; the rules for combining words into phrases and sentences are syntax.
Language is slower to develop in boys, twins, large families, social classes 4 and 5, and those lacking speech stimulation (e.g. deaf and neglected children).

Pre-linguistic stage (0 to 12 months): crying is an important form of communication; a one-month-old can distinguish speech sounds (categorical speech perception, supposed innate). Cooing by six weeks; babbling by six months (repetitive production of speech sounds; spontaneous babbling = enjoying making sounds alone). All babies babble at about the same age irrespective of culture; deaf babies of deaf-mute parents also babble but stop at 9 to 10 months. Phonemic expansion = production of phonemes even if absent from the native language.

One-word stage (12 to 18 months): jargon and babbling continue to 18 months; first words are often self-invented but consistently carry the same meaning, with clear intention to communicate. Earliest words are context bound (performatives; 'teddy' said only when teddy is thrown up refers to the action). Holophrases are one-word substitutes for whole phrases or sentences. Child understands more words than it produces. Words then decontextualise into five functions: nominals (specific e.g. Sarah, or general e.g. ball pen), action words (e.g. bye, look), function words (e.g. the, for, what - prepositions and grammatical functions), modifiers (e.g. red, big), and personal and social words (e.g. oops, ouch).
Two-word sentences / stage 1 grammar (18 to 30 months): telegraphic speech - meaningful words used without connecting words. At this stage adults interact with children in 'motherese'.

Motherese is short, simple, raised-pitch paraphrased language directed at infants. As object permanence is achieved, words start to have representational functions. Stage 2 grammar (over 30 months): mean length of utterance increases largely through function words.

blocks.title: Theories of language acquisition
rows: Children are born with an innate language acquisition device; transformational grammar is important. Every language has a surface structure (accurate syntax, actual words) and a deep structure (most semantic sense, without similar syntactical rules); a single surface structure can have several deep structures. Children are born equipped with the ability to decipher the transformational grammar of deep to surface structure conversion; hence years up to puberty are sensitive though not critical for language development.
Adults such as the mother act as **language acquisition support system**, essential since the function of language is social interaction.

blocks.text: Freud: boys' unconscious wish to compete with the father leads to castration anxiety, repression and identification with the father, from whom the superego morality is incorporated. In girls the Oedipus complex is not seen; instead penis envy (Electra complex) with the father as love object and an unconscious wish for his baby; without strong anxiety, identification with the mother and superego occur. Freud therefore claimed superego/morality is weaker in women than men.

Piaget described qualitative differences between older and younger children in morality, based on older children's social perspective (an extension of Theory of Mind); he did not describe stage-by-stage development of morality. Cognitive development is essential but not sufficient for moral development; moral development lags 2 years behind cognitive development.

blocks.title: Piaget's moral development theory
rows: Unilateral respect for the external law: seniors make rules; they are sacred and should not be broken, but get violated periodically for pleasure
Mutual respect for the self-invented law: can be changed by consensus and for fairness
External responsibility holds for crime; severity of outcome or loss decides the punishment
Internal responsibility holds for crime; intent/motivation decides the punishment
Moral realism: strong penalty for any crime; can accept collective punishment to deliver justice (punishing the wrongdoer is more important than not hurting the innocent)
Moral relativism: punishment should match the crime; does not accept collective punishment
Immanent justice: the world is just - a misfortune will punish the deserved for a misdeed
Heteronomous morality: subject to rules written by others
Autonomous morality: rules can be self-made

blocks.text: Kohlberg: a stagewise process studying the reasons (more important than the judgment itself) for decisions in hypothetical dilemmas (Heinz Dilemma); 3 levels and 6 stages.

blocks.title: Kohlberg's levels and stages
rows: Level 1 Pre-conventional (7-12 years to middle childhood)
Obedience to rules to avoid punishment
What brings rewards is right; 'tit for tat'
What pleases others/the majority is right; conforms to avoid disapproval and meet expectations of others; being good, having good motives and showing concern are important
iv. Social order or authority orientation
Upholds laws and social rules to avoid censure of authorities and guilt; maintaining social order is the goal
v. Social contract or legalistic orientation
Principles agreed by the group as essential to public welfare; democracy upheld; individual life given more respect than written law

Actions guided by self-chosen ethical principles; laws and social principles are usually valid because they are based on these principles; social rules can be broken if universal morality is not upheld

blocks.text: Level 1 (pre-conventional): children decide right or wrong according to the consequences - if an action leads to punishment it must be bad, if it leads to reward it must be good. Level 2 (conventional): social rules and the expectations of others determine what is acceptable or unacceptable behaviour. Level 3 (post-conventional): what is right is based on the individual's understanding of universal ethical principles - often abstract and ill-defined, but may include the preservation of life at all costs and the importance of human dignity.

Eisenberg's stages are based on prosocial reasoning (helping or altruistic behaviour), whereas Kohlberg's and Piaget's theories were based on prohibition of the wrong.

blocks.text: Emotional literacy is used interchangeably with emotional intelligence (Steiner, 1997). Components: knowing your feelings; having a sense of empathy; learning to manage our emotions; repairing emotional problems; emotional interactivity - putting it together.

Emotion regulation is the ability to gauge the appropriate level of emotional response and respond to stimuli with a range of emotions in a controlled manner (Panfile and Laible 2012). Infants have limited regulation (gaze aversion, vocalising); around 1 year children can unconsciously regulate emotions; at 3 to 5 years they may tolerate ordinary brief frustrations and handle minor disappointments. Emotion regulation develops throughout the lifespan (Cole et al., 2009).

blocks.text: Gender identity typically forms around age 3-4 and remains established. Gender typing is the process by which an individual acquires gender-related traits within their society. It usually starts with clothing at a young age. Gender role is the behaviour an individual engages in that identifies with their gender (e.g. use of cosmetics).

blocks.title: Theories of gender identity development
rows: Girls and boys behave differently because society treats them differently; fathers treat children in a more gendered way than mothers; sex typing is reinforced by observational learning and reinforcement for accomplishing gender-specific tasks.
The child's own participation matters; discovery of biological sex leads to identification with a group and conformity.
Gender identity alone provides the motivation to assume sex-typed behaviour; children observe and learn to be a specific gender, and the culture's gender schema becomes a standard for comparison.

blocks.text: Buying dolls for girls and cars for boys is **SOCIAL** **LEARNING** (reinforcement and modelling, first through parents; e.g. parents discourage sons from dolls more than daughters from trucks) — not gender schema, imprinting, self-realisation or cognitive mapping.

Sex drive exists from birth but increases in adolescence due to raised androgen secretion. Sexual orientation is explored during adolescence; there are arguments for and against biological determination vs shaping in childhood.

sections.title: 17. Adaptations in adolescence and adult life

blocks.text: Adolescence is the period between childhood and adulthood (Piaget - formal operational, Freud - genital stage, Erikson - identity vs. role confusion). Conflict with parents is common due to developing a sense of self and autonomy, attributed to a second separation-individuation phase.

Anna Freud described affective instability: oscillation between behavioural and affective excess and scarcity during adolescence, induced by endocrine changes, sexual maturity and instability of ego defenses.

Erikson described adolescent turmoil as a temporary maladaptive state due to identity diffusion, passed through by all adolescents. Offer & Offer (1975) showed upheaval is common but need not occur in all: nearly ==23%== showed continuous linear development; ==35%== were late bloomers (less introspective, some friction with families); around ==21%== had recurrent conflicts with parents and chose less competitive careers.

Marcia's theory: a mature self-identity is possible only if an individual experiences several crises, finally arriving at a stage of commitment. Successful maturation during adolescence depends on both the degree of crises faced and the commitment achieved.

blocks.text: Risk-taking behaviour (and negative identity) is **LESS** common in societies that mark the transition to adulthood by initiation ceremonies; delinquency peaks in the late teens (about 17) and declines afterwards — **NOT** in the early teens, which is the wrong-peak distractor.

blocks.text: Pairing occurs often within the same cultural and socioeconomic background (homogamous mate selection). Equity theory: individuals weigh the cost-benefit ratio for each person in a relationship; reinforcement theory: partners are chosen on the basis of reinforcement of attraction with rewards.

Midlife transition occurs around age 40 to 45. 'Midlife crisis' was coined by Elliot Jacques - a critical phase between the forties and early sixties, often associated with realising mortality, unrealized goals, menopause or children leaving home.
Downshifting = voluntarily opting out of a pressurized career and giving up a well-paid job for a more fulfilling life (anti-urbanism); empty nest distress = loneliness when children leave home.
Bereavement can refer to loss of anything (marriage, employment) and is a state of mourning, a process influenced by culture and society in which grief is resolved.

Lindemann (1944; 101 bereaved people): after an unexpected death, initial shock lasts 10-14 days, then intense sadness with possible social withdrawal, then anger (protest), and within a year or so grief is resolved. These stages were refined by Parkes.

blocks.title: Parkes: 5 stages of bereavement
rows: Illusions or hallucinations of the deceased can occur

blocks.text: 'Protest' is the stage in Lindemann's sequence (shock for 10-14 days, then intense sadness with possible withdrawal, then anger as the bereaved 'protests', then resolution within about a year); mourning, acting out, ambivalence and bargaining are distractors not in that pattern.

Stress in pregnancy: placental release of corticotrophin releasing hormone increases with stress, with increased risk of intrauterine infection, preterm labour and low birth weight. Pre-term infants are susceptible to developmental delay and increased mortality; babies stressed in utero can have difficult temperament and be irritable, and have increased risk of chronic health issues in adulthood (e.g. hypertension, diabetes).

After childbirth: intrusive thoughts, avoidance, anxiety, depression, social dysfunction and somatisation. Significant psychological distress is noted in ==37%== of mothers and ==13%== of fathers; predictors of acute maternal distress include being a single parent, multiparity and previous traumatic birth. At six weeks and six months distress fell to general population level, indicating mostly short-term distress.

A child builds a tower of 6 cubes at 2 years; at 3 years a tower of 9-10 cubes.
An 8-year-old (6-11 years) is in **INDUSTRY** vs **INFERIORITY**; the outcome is a sense of achievement or inadequacy.

blocks.text: Age is the first social category learnt by a child, even before number concept develops.
Cognition: brain mass reduces with ageing; memory (particularly working memory and incidental memory) is the cognitive function most often cited as susceptible to decline; attention also declines.
Physiology: bone loss reduces mechanical strength, collagen fibres deteriorate causing loss of skin elasticity, and organ efficacy deteriorates.

Socioeconomic independence: older adults are economically vulnerable and may outlive their financial resources; declining socio-economic status can worsen physical and mental health; reduced mobility impacts independence and social ties.

blocks.title: Theories of role change in old age
rows: Mutual withdrawal of society and the individual; increased individuality and shrinking life space are inevitable moves towards death.
An ageist society reduces social interaction; withdrawal is not mutual but forced.
Age robs people of the ability to engage in reciprocal roles; retirement is a social contract exchanging productivity for increased leisure and decreased responsibilities.
Wise investment of social energy in old age is to limit interaction to those most familiar.

blocks.title: Phases of retirement
rows: Increasing anxiety with the retirement of friends and colleagues
Immediate post-retirement phase where increased freedom is enjoyed
Slowing down occurs, feels let down; worse if inadequately prepared for retirement
Makes choices; mastery attained in chosen leisure

Ageing: reduced brain mass; memory (working, incidental) most susceptible; attention declines.

blocks.text: Brain development is genetically programmed; cortical thickness in lateral prefrontal, medial prefrontal, parietal and temporal cortices is highly heritable. Regions crucial for evolutionarily advanced functions (higher-order cognition, sociality, language) show both high heritability and increasing heritability with age, similar to **intelligence quotient** - either age-dependent gene expression or gene-environment interaction.

Gene-environment interaction: e.g. phenylketonuria (lack of the enzyme that breaks down phenylalanine, causing intellectual disability) can be managed with phenylalanine-free foods, resulting in normal development.

blocks.title: Concepts in developmental genetics
rows: Some behaviour traits are strongly genetically determined (canalized, e.g. crawling) so development follows them; others are poorly canalized (e.g. cycling) so environment influences them. Some traits are heavily canalized early (language development) but less so later (reading ability).
Genes do not shape behaviour in its entirety; they only set limits (a range) within which individual variability is shaped by the environment.
Genes contribute to propensities toward certain skills; children then seek activities compatible with their genetic endowment.

blocks.title: Three types of gene-environment interaction (Reviewer correction (not in the source): standard term is gene-environment correlation - passive, evocative, active)
rows: Environment influenced by parental genes, which are correlated with the child's genes; phenotype results from environmental influences indirectly associated with parental genes
A boy who does not inherit his father's tallness may still become a good basketball player through repeated exposure to basketball sessions
Environment influenced by genetically shaped behaviour of the child; environmental influences are evoked by the child's own genes
A girl who inherits impulsivity may evoke an abusive parental reaction, leading to later depression (depression itself not inherited)
Environment influenced by the child's active choice to complement genetically shaped interests
A girl who inherits impulsivity may choose to gamble, losses leading to later depression (depression itself not inherited)

bullets.text: Cortical thickness in prefrontal, parietal and temporal cortices is highly heritable; heritability of higher-order regions rises with age.

blocks.text: Neural tube is seen 2-3 weeks after formation of the human fetus; by week 5 ectodermal tissues differentiate to precursors of brain regions; then birth of neurons from stem cells (ventricular proliferative zone, by week 8), neuronal migration (weeks 12-20), formation and pruning of axons, dendrites and synaptic contacts, myelination, and apoptotic removal of excess cells.

blocks.title: Fetal neurodevelopment timeline
rows: Transient cortical subplate of migrating neurons visible beneath the cortex; withers by 20 weeks, replaced by permanent cortical sheet at 24 to 28 weeks (migration is one of the earliest events visible on neuroimaging)
Cortical folding (sulci and gyri) visible on fetal **magnetic resonance imaging**

Neuronal count at peak - around ==40%== greater than in the adult; dendritic formation accelerates (cannot be seen on magnetic resonance imaging); proliferative zone and cortical subplate disappear; cortical thickness increase notable on fetal **magnetic resonance imaging**
Synaptogenesis peaks (~40,000 new synapses formed per second); continues postnatally alongside synapse elimination; net synapse number begins to decrease at puberty (pruning)

blocks.text: Synaptic pruning cannot be observed directly with neuroimaging, but progressive cortical thinning of frontal and parietal cortices on **magnetic resonance imaging** in adolescence is attributed to it; an indirect indicator of synaptic removal is glucose metabolism measured by **positron emission tomography**.

Myelination of visual cortical white matter begins prenatally (last trimester); by 9 months postnatal, myelination extends to frontal cortex (posterior-to-anterior maturation: sensory pathways, then motor pathways, finally higher-order association areas).

blocks.title: National Institute of Mental Health (United States) longitudinal studies of brain volumes in children
rows: Volume increases linearly up to age 20 years in all brain regions
Frontal, parietal and temporal volumes follow an inverted-U curve (increase before adolescence; frontoparietal peak at 12 years, temporal peak at 16 years; universal reduction thereafter)

Decreases with age in a back-to-front progression: sensorimotor areas first, then dorsal parietal, superior temporal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortices - sensorimotor areas mature earlier than higher-order regions

blocks.text: Cortical thinning may be due to synaptic pruning or myelination (with myelination, tissue identified as white matter on **magnetic resonance imaging** increases in proportion, reducing relative grey matter thickness).

Diffusion Tensor Imaging (integrity of white matter tracts): directionality of diffusion continues to increase with age especially in prefrontal regions and basal ganglia, suggesting frontostriatal systems myelinate progressively during adolescence; frontotemporal pathways may continue to myelinate until age 30 years.

**magnetic resonance** spectroscopy: N-acetyl-aspartate (indicator of neuronal integrity) is low around birth, rises rapidly during the first 2 years, then slows; may represent synaptogenesis in childhood. Functional **magnetic resonance imaging**: age-related increases in activation of left frontal and temporal cortices (language areas) support expansion of reading and phonological skills.
